title: Air India Adds First Class to Sydney, Lifts Delhi Flights to 11 Weekly
excerpt: Sydney-Delhi goes from daily to 11 flights a week with first-class Boeing 777s from December, Melbourne gets the same frequency lift, and Delhi connections drop to 60 minutes.
body:
• Air India will lift Sydney-Delhi flights from 7 to 11 a week, with Boeing 777-300ER aircraft on selected services from 5 December 2026 and on all Sydney flights from 1 January 2027.
  • The 777 brings first class to the Sydney route for the first time — eight private suites — plus 40 flat-bed business seats in a 1-2-1 layout, up from 18 business seats on the current 787-8.
  • Melbourne passengers have had the upgraded 777 product since July, and Melbourne-Delhi frequencies are also rising to 11 a week.
  • For travellers connecting beyond Delhi, Air India's Easy Connect cuts the minimum connection to 60 minutes, down from three hours, with bags checked through to Varanasi, Amritsar and Ahmedabad — check the aircraft type for your date before booking on Air India's Sydney booking page.

Air India is expanding in Australia, adding flights and a first-class cabin on its Sydney-Delhi route and signalling that more Australian cities could follow once new widebody aircraft arrive. The changes, outlined by the airline's head of global sales, Manish Puri, at a media briefing in Melbourne this week, mark 70 years of Air India services between Australia and India, according to Executive Traveller.

What Changes in Sydney and Melbourne

Sydney is the headline upgrade. Selected Sydney-Delhi services switch to the larger Boeing 777-300ER from 5 December 2026, and the type takes over the whole route from 1 January 2027, replacing the Boeing 787-8. Weekly frequencies rise from seven to 11 — a 57 percent increase that Sydney Airport estimates adds roughly 170,000 seats a year.

The cabin change is substantial. The 777s, previously flown by Etihad Airways, carry eight first-class private suites, 40 business-class flat beds in a direct-aisle 1-2-1 arrangement and 280 economy seats. The 787-8 they replace offers just 18 business seats in a 2-2-2 layout and no first class. Melbourne travellers have had the 777 product since July, and the airline says both Australian routes are moving from daily services to 11 flights a week, with Melbourne's increase due from late October.

"This is a big game changer."

— Manish Puri, Air India Head of Global Sales, on Easy Connect

Why Australia, Why Now

Puri described Australia as a strategic market with strong, sustained demand and unusually strong demand for premium cabins. Corporate travellers currently account for almost 10 percent of the airline's Australian business, he said, and Air India expects that share to climb toward 25 percent as the new product reaches Melbourne and, in the first quarter of next year, Sydney. The airline says it already holds about a 30 percent share of business-class traffic and a 24 percent overall share on its Australian routes.

The expansion sits inside a wider transformation. Air India is in the final phase of a five-year programme, has ordered 600 Airbus and Boeing aircraft, and expects more than 100 new aircraft to join over the next two years, taking the Air India Group fleet past 400 by the end of 2028. About half its twin-aisle fleet is now new or refurbished, with a target of 75 percent by the end of 2027.

The Connection Play Beyond Delhi

Around 35 percent of Air India's Australian passengers travel beyond Delhi, and 12 percent travel beyond India altogether. That is the market Easy Connect targets. Eligible passengers check bags through to their final Indian destination and complete customs and immigration there, rather than collecting luggage and rechecking at Delhi. The minimum connection falls from three hours to 60 minutes.

The scheme covers Varanasi, Amritsar and Ahmedabad today, with 10 to 12 more cities expected in the next six months, subject to government approval. Puri cited Melbourne-Amritsar as early evidence: Air India's share on that connecting market rose from 32 percent in September, when the hub-and-spoke push began, to 55 percent. Travellers can review the airline's Australian routes on its flights to Australia page.

What Comes Next

Brisbane has been reported as under consideration, and Puri did not rule out the new Western Sydney International Airport, saying the airline will keep exploring capacity with partners. His stated priority, though, is densifying the existing network first. New cities, he indicated, depend on widebody deliveries. For the large Indian community in Sydney and Melbourne — students, families visiting relatives and business travellers — the immediate gain is more concrete: more weekly choices, a genuine first-class option, and a Delhi connection that no longer consumes half a day.
